summary.text: Systems of linear equations and inequalities: the vocabulary (system, solution, inconsistent system), solving by substitution and elimination, the three possible outcomes, systems of linear inequalities as shaded regions, and extending the method to three variables.

why.text: Almost every real modelling problem has more than one condition at once — a budget and a time limit, a number of coins and their value. Systems are how those conditions get written down together, and the difference between one solution, none, and infinitely many is a genuinely useful thing to recognise on sight.

objectives.text: Solve a two-variable linear system by substitution or elimination and check the result.
Recognise from the algebra or the graph whether a system has one solution, none, or infinitely many.
Write a system of inequalities from real constraints and describe the solution region.
Solve a system of three equations in three variables by eliminating one variable first.
Choose between substitution and elimination by looking at the coefficients.

parentNote.text: Built from the enVision Lesson 1-6 textbook pages, with fresh questions so the practice sheets stay usable as homework. The recurring errors here are writing an ordered pair backwards and treating a proportional second equation as if it were new information — both have their own question. The word problems (coins, tiles, the saline mixture, the basketball scores) are the ones most likely to need a second pass; each has a full walkthrough.

nextUp.text: The vocabulary cards are quick, and worth doing first — several questions turn on knowing exactly what "inconsistent" means. Then take the quiz.

cards.def:
**Two or more linear equations that share the same variables.**
• The equations are considered together, not one at a time.
• Braces are the usual notation for grouping them.
cards.hint: A system is a set of conditions that must all hold at once.

cards.def:
**Every ordered pair (or triple) that makes ALL the equations true at the same time.**
• Satisfying one equation is not enough.
• Graphically, it is where all the graphs meet.
cards.hint: All equations, simultaneously — that is the whole idea.

cards.def:
**One solution, no solution, or infinitely many.**
• Lines crossing once: one solution.
• Parallel lines: none — an inconsistent system.
• The same line twice: infinitely many.
cards.hint: Two lines can cross, miss, or coincide. Nothing else.

cards.def:
**A system with no solution at all.**
• Solving produces a false statement such as 0 = 6.
• Graphically the lines are parallel.
cards.hint: A contradiction with no variable left means no solution.

cards.def:
**Solve one equation for one variable, then put that expression into the other equation.**
• Best when a variable already stands alone or has coefficient 1.
• Leaves a single equation in a single variable.
cards.hint: Trade one variable away and the rest is ordinary algebra.

cards.def:
**Add or subtract multiples of the equations so one variable cancels.**
• Multiplying an equation by a nonzero number does not change its solutions.
• Neither does replacing one equation with the sum of the two.
cards.hint: Line up a variable with opposite coefficients and add.

cards.def:
**Two or more inequalities in the same variables, solved together.**
• The solution is a REGION of the plane, not a single point.
• Any point in the shaded overlap satisfies all of them.
cards.hint: Equations give points. Inequalities give territory.

cards.def:
**Pick a point not on the boundary, substitute it, and shade the side that makes the inequality true.**
• (0, 0) is the easiest test point when the boundary misses the origin.
• Repeat for each inequality; the overlap is the answer.
cards.hint: One substitution tells you which side of the line to shade.

cards.def:
**Each real-world limit becomes one inequality.**
• At least $200 at $20 and $10 per hour: 20x + 10y ≥ 200.
• At most 20 hours total: x + y ≤ 20.
• At least 5 hours walking dogs: y ≥ 5.
cards.hint: "At least" is ≥. "At most" is ≤. Translate one phrase at a time.

cards.def:
**Eliminate one variable to get a two-variable system, then solve that the usual way.**
• Combine equations in pairs so the same variable disappears from each pair.
• Back-substitute to recover the variable you removed.
cards.hint: Reduce three to two, solve two, then work backwards.

cards.def:
**Once you have one variable, put it back into the simplest equation to find the next.**
• Work back through the chain until every variable is known.
• The answer for three variables is an ordered triple.
cards.hint: Solve the easiest thing last-first, then walk back up.

cards.def:
**Substitute your answer into EVERY original equation, not just the one you used.**
• A pair that satisfies only one equation is not a solution.
• This is the single most common way a wrong answer survives.
cards.hint: One equation agreeing proves nothing. Check them all.

cards.def:
**x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 restrict the solution to the first quadrant.**
• They usually appear because a quantity cannot be negative — hours, items, distances.
• They are real constraints and must be graphed.
cards.hint: You cannot work −3 hours, so the model has to say so.

cards.def:
**A region is far easier to see than to describe, and the corners of that region are where the best answers usually sit.**
• Overlapping shading shows every combination that works at once.
• Listing them algebraically would be endless.
cards.hint: Some answers are easier to draw than to write.

questions.q: What is the solution of a system of linear equations?
opts: Any pair that satisfies at least one equation
Every pair that satisfies all the equations at the same time
The point where a line crosses the x-axis
The slopes of the two lines
questions.hint: The word "system" means the equations are taken together.
steps: A system is several equations sharing the same variables.
A solution has to make every one of them true simultaneously.
Graphically that is the point where all the graphs meet.

ex.main: **Every pair that satisfies all the equations at the same time.** Satisfying one and failing another is not a solution.
ex.tip: Always verify a candidate against every equation in the system.

questions.q: Solve the system: x + 2y = 3 and x − 2y = 4.
questions.hint: Adding the two equations removes y immediately.
steps: Add the equations: (x + 2y) + (x − 2y) = 3 + 4 gives 2x = 7, so x = 7/2.
Substitute into x + 2y = 3: 7/2 + 2y = 3, so 2y = −1/2 and y = −1/4.
The solution is (7/2, −1/4). Check in the second: 7/2 − 2(−1/4) = 7/2 + 1/2 = 4. ✓

ex.main: **(7/2, −1/4).** Opposite coefficients on y make elimination by adding the fastest route here.
ex.tip: Scan for a variable whose coefficients are already opposites before doing any work.

questions.q: Solving a system produces the statement 0 = 6. What does that mean?
opts: The system has infinitely many solutions
questions.hint: Is 0 = 6 ever true?
steps: Every step so far kept the solutions unchanged.
The variables have all cancelled and what remains, 0 = 6, is false.
No values can make it true, so the system has no solution — it is inconsistent, and the lines are parallel.

ex.main: **The system has no solution.** A false numeric statement with no variables left is the signature of an inconsistent system.
ex.tip: If instead you land on something always true, like 0 = 0, there are infinitely many solutions.

questions.q: Solve the system: 2x + 2y = 10 and x + 5y = 13.
questions.hint: Divide the first equation by 2 to make substitution easy.
steps: Divide the first by 2: x + y = 5, so x = 5 − y.
Substitute: (5 − y) + 5y = 13, giving 4y = 8 and y = 2.

ex.main: **(3, 2).** Simplifying an equation before substituting saves most of the arithmetic.
ex.tip: Divide out a common factor first — it makes every later step smaller.

questions.q: In a system of inequalities, what do the constraints x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 do?
opts: They restrict the solution to the first quadrant
They shift the boundary lines up
They have no effect on the solution
questions.hint: Where on the plane are both coordinates non-negative?
steps: x ≥ 0 keeps the region on or right of the y-axis.
y ≥ 0 keeps it on or above the x-axis.
Together they confine the solution to the first quadrant, which is usually there because a quantity cannot be negative.

ex.main: **They restrict the solution to the first quadrant.** They are genuine constraints, not decoration — hours worked and items sold cannot be negative.
ex.tip: If a variable counts something real, expect a non-negativity constraint.

questions.q: Shandra says (−1, 2) solves the system 2x + y = 3 and −x + 4y = −6. Is she right?
opts: No — it fails both equations; the solution is (2, −1)
No — it satisfies the first but not the second
No — the system has no solution
questions.hint: Substitute into the first equation before anything else.
steps: Test the first: 2(−1) + 2 = 0, but the equation needs 3. It already fails.
Solve properly: y = 3 − 2x, so −x + 4(3 − 2x) = −6 gives −9x = −18 and x = 2.
Then y = 3 − 4 = −1, so the solution is (2, −1). Shandra reversed the coordinates.

ex.main: **No — the solution is (2, −1).** Writing an ordered pair backwards is one of the most common errors in this topic.
ex.tip: Order matters: (a, b) is not (b, a). Check with a substitution every time.

questions.q: Solve: x = 2y − 5 and 3x − y = 5.
questions.hint: The first equation already has x alone — substitute it.
steps: Substitute x = 2y − 5 into 3x − y = 5: 3(2y − 5) − y = 5.

ex.main: **(3, 4).** When a variable is already isolated, substitution is almost always the quickest method.
ex.tip: Pick your method by looking at the system, not by habit.

questions.q: Solve: x − 3y = 1 and 2x − y = 7.
questions.hint: Solve the first for x, then substitute.
steps: From x − 3y = 1, x = 1 + 3y.
Substitute: 2(1 + 3y) − y = 7, so 2 + 5y = 7 and y = 1.

ex.main: **(4, 1).** A coefficient of 1 on x is an invitation to substitute.
ex.tip: Isolating a variable with coefficient 1 avoids fractions entirely.

questions.q: A system contains 3x + 2y = 5 and 6x + 4y = 3. How many solutions does it have?
questions.hint: Compare the two equations after doubling the first.
steps: Double the first equation: 6x + 4y = 10.
The second says 6x + 4y = 3. The same expression cannot equal both 10 and 3.
The lines are parallel and the system is inconsistent, so there are no solutions.

ex.main: **None.** Matching left sides with different right sides is the algebraic picture of parallel lines.
ex.tip: Proportional coefficients with a non-matching constant always means parallel.

questions.q: Charles has 8 coins, all dimes and quarters, worth $1.25. How many quarters does he have?
questions.hint: Write one equation for the count and one for the value in cents.
steps: Let d be dimes and q quarters: d + q = 8 and 10d + 25q = 125.
From the first, d = 8 − q. Substitute: 10(8 − q) + 25q = 125.

ex.main: **3 quarters.** Coin problems always give two equations: how many, and how much.
ex.tip: Work in cents to keep the value equation free of decimals.

questions.q: A set of triangular and square tiles has 50 pieces and 170 sides in total. How many square tiles are there?
questions.hint: Triangles contribute 3 sides each, squares 4.
steps: Let t be triangles and s squares: t + s = 50 and 3t + 4s = 170.
From the first, t = 50 − s. Substitute: 3(50 − s) + 4s = 170.
150 + s = 170, so s = 20 squares (and 30 triangles). Check: 3(30) + 4(20) = 170 ✓

ex.main: **20 squares.** The side count is what separates the two shapes; the piece count alone cannot.
ex.tip: When two things differ by one property, that property gives the second equation.

questions.q: Malcolm earns $20/h mowing and $10/h walking dogs. He wants at least $200, can work at most 20 hours, and must walk dogs at least 5 hours. Which system models this?
questions.hint: "At least" points one way, "at most" the other.
steps: Earnings of at least $200 at those rates: 20x + 10y ≥ 200.
A maximum of 20 hours in total: x + y ≤ 20.
A minimum of 5 hours with the dogs: y ≥ 5.

ex.main: **20x + 10y ≥ 200, x + y ≤ 20, y ≥ 5.** Each phrase in the problem becomes exactly one inequality, and the direction comes from the wording.
ex.tip: Underline "at least" and "at most" before writing anything.

questions.q: Raul earns $75 per week plus $5 per membership. A new gym offers $50 per week plus $7.50 per membership. How many memberships make the new gym better?
questions.hint: Set the new pay above the old pay and solve.
steps: New pay: 50 + 7.5m. Old pay: 75 + 5m.
The new gym is better when 50 + 7.5m > 75 + 5m.
2.5m > 25, so m > 10. At exactly 10 memberships both pay $125.

ex.main: **More than 10.** The lower base pay is repaid by the higher rate, and 10 is the break-even point.
ex.tip: Break-even is where the two expressions are equal; the inequality picks the side.

questions.q: Solve the three-variable system: 2x + y − z = −10, −x + 2y + z = 3, x + 2y + 3z = 13.
questions.hint: Adding the first two equations removes z straight away.
steps: Add equations one and two: x + 3y = −7.
Multiply equation two by −3 and add to equation three to eliminate z as well, giving 4x − 4y = 4, so x = y + 1.
Substitute: (y + 1) + 3y = −7 gives y = −2 and x = −1. Back-substitute into the first: 2(−1) + (−2) − z = −10, so z = 6.

ex.main: **(−1, −2, 6).** Three variables become two by eliminating the same variable from two different pairs.
ex.tip: Choose the variable that is easiest to cancel, then be consistent about it.

questions.q: Pilar scored 26 points. She made 2 more free throws (1 point) than 2-point baskets, and 4 times as many free throws as 3-point baskets. How many 3-pointers did she make?
questions.hint: Let the 3-pointers be the unknown everything else is described by.
steps: Let h be 3-pointers. Free throws f = 4h, and 2-point baskets t = f − 2 = 4h − 2.
Total points: f + 2t + 3h = 26, so 4h + 2(4h − 2) + 3h = 26.
4h + 8h − 4 + 3h = 26 gives 15h = 30, so h = 2. That is 8 free throws, 6 two-pointers and 2 three-pointers: 8 + 12 + 6 = 26 ✓

ex.main: **2 three-pointers.** Naming the most-referenced quantity as the variable turns three unknowns into one.
ex.tip: Let the variable be whatever the other quantities are described in terms of.

questions.q: Ramona needs 10 mL of a 30% saline solution, mixing a 50% and a 25% solution. How much of the 50% does she need?
questions.hint: One equation for total volume, one for total salt.
steps: Let x be mL of the 50% and y of the 25%: x + y = 10.
Substitute y = 10 − x: 0.5x + 2.5 − 0.25x = 3, so 0.25x = 0.5 and x = 2 mL (with 8 mL of the 25%).

ex.main: **2 mL of the 50% solution.** Mixture problems always pair a volume equation with a content equation.
ex.tip: The target concentration is closer to 25%, so most of the mixture must be the weaker one.

questions.q: For what value of a is (−1, 1) the solution of the system 3x + 5y = 2 and ax + 8y = 14?
questions.hint: Substitute the known solution into the second equation.
steps: First confirm the point fits equation one: 3(−1) + 5(1) = 2 ✓
Substitute into the second: a(−1) + 8(1) = 14.

ex.main: **a = −6.** A given solution turns an unknown coefficient into a one-step substitution.
ex.tip: Check the point against the complete equation first — it confirms you have the right point.

questions.q: One equation of a system with exactly one solution is 4x + 2y = 14. Which could be the second equation?
questions.hint: A second equation proportional to the first cannot give exactly one solution.
steps: Exactly one solution means the two lines have different slopes.
2x + y = 7, 8x + 4y = 28 and 6x + 3y = 21 are all just 4x + 2y = 14 rescaled — each is the same line, giving infinitely many solutions.
−3x + 10y = 1 has a different slope, so it crosses the first line exactly once.

ex.main: **−3x + 10y = 1.** The others are all multiples of the given equation, which describes the same line rather than a second one.
ex.tip: Compare the ratio of coefficients: equal ratios mean the same line or a parallel one.

questions.q: A system of inequalities describes a shaded region rather than a point. Why?
opts: Because every point in the overlap satisfies all the inequalities at once
Because the boundary lines are always parallel
Because the region is only an estimate of the real answer
questions.hint: How many pairs satisfy x + y ≤ 20 on its own?
steps: An inequality is satisfied by every point on one side of its boundary, not just the boundary itself.
With several inequalities, the points satisfying all of them are where the shaded sides overlap.
That overlap is usually a whole region, and any point inside it is a genuine solution.

ex.main: **Because every point in the overlap satisfies all the inequalities at once.** Equations pin down points; inequalities allow territory.
ex.tip: The corners of the region are where the best answers usually sit in real problems.

questions.q: Keisha designs a rectangular enclosure at most 125 m long, using at most 300 m of fencing, with the length at least double the width. Which system models it?
questions.hint: Perimeter of a rectangle is 2x + 2y, and "at least double" points one way.
steps: Length at most 125 m: y ≤ 125.
At most 300 m of fencing is a perimeter constraint: 2x + 2y ≤ 300.
The length is at least double the width: y ≥ 2x.

ex.main: **y ≤ 125, 2x + 2y ≤ 300, y ≥ 2x.** Fencing is a perimeter, so both pairs of sides count.
ex.tip: A fencing budget is almost always a perimeter, not a length.
